title: In the midst of life (1662)
hookLine: the burial service: in the midst of life we are in death
tomorrow: what if prayer is closer to hanging out than to a speech?

cards: Funerals now come in more than one style. Some are called a celebration of life, with slideshows, favorite songs and laughter. Others keep the older shape: dark clothes, slow music, tears allowed.

The 1662 prayer book has words for the graveside itself, said as the body is made ready to be laid in the earth: "In the midst of life we are in death." That's what it gives people to say at the edge of a grave.
And Christians don't all lean on it the same way.

teach.h: NOT AT THE END; IN THE MIDDLE.
teach.b: Here's the whole sentence, from the Burial of the Dead: "In the midst of life we are in death: of whom may we seek for succour, but of thee, O Lord, who for our sins art justly displeased?"
Not at the end of life; in the middle of it. Then, at once, a question that holds its own answer: who can we go to for help? Thee.
Two voices lean on this service differently.
The first says: name death plainly. Keep it in view, as a psalm asks: "So teach us to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom." Grief gets room, and nobody hurries past the grave.

The second voice says: lead with hope. The same service reads Paul's letter to the Corinthians, with its taunt: "O death, where is thy sting? O grave, where is thy victory?" So celebrate the life, and sing.
The first: hope that skips the grief rings hollow to the people grieving. The second: grief without hope forgets what the service is for.
And the service holds both in one handful of earth, said as it falls on the coffin: "earth to earth, ashes to ashes, dust to dust; in sure and certain hope of the Resurrection to eternal life."

how: In the 1662 Book of Common Prayer these words are said or sung at the graveside; Anglican and Episcopal funerals still use them or later versions, and some Christian funerals are planned as a celebration of life.

games.q: what does “in the midst of life” mean?
o: a saying that life is short, so enjoy it now
a promise that no one will ever really die
a graveside line: death named, then help asked of God

games.q: in the midst of life — tap the pairs.
p: that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom

s: the line is mainly a grim reminder that death is coming
the likely reading. it names death, then turns at once to ask God for help, and the service sets hope beside it.
the same burial service reads Paul's 'O death, where is thy sting?'
from Paul's first letter to the Corinthians.
Christians all agree on whether a funeral should lead with grief or with hope
some lean on naming death plainly, others on celebrating hope; the service holds both.

games.q: your family is planning a funeral. your aunt wants a celebration of life, all stories and bright songs. you lean toward the older shape, with room to grieve. what's her best case?
o: grief without hope forgets what the service is for.
sad funerals are old-fashioned and should be dropped.
if people cry, it means they don't really believe.
games.why: the 1662 service reads 'O death, where is thy sting?' and lays the body in the earth in sure and certain hope. hope is her case; room to grieve is yours. the service keeps both.

practice: Look at one thing that won't last: a cut flower, a fallen leaf, a candle, a photo of someone who has died. Let your eyes rest on it without pressing any thought hard.
If someone you loved has died, you can say their name softly; if you pray, the psalm's line is there: so teach us to number our days.

wordCard.voice: In the midst of life. The graveside line that names death, then turns at once to ask God for help.

orig.note: Latin for in the midst of life. tradition says the English line grew from an old Latin chant.

carryVoice: Here's your line: in the midst of life, where dust and hope share one handful of earth. Go gently.
